subtopic: Irrational Numbers and the Number Line
stem: Prove that \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number, using indirect proof.
solution:
Let us assume that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational. So \(\sqrt{2}\) can be expressed in \(\frac{p}{q}\) form.

\(\frac{p}{q}\) is the reduced form of a rational number, hence \(p\) and \(q\) have no common factor other than 1.

\(\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}\)

\(\therefore 2=\frac{p^{2}}{q^{2}}\)  (Squaring both the sides)

\(\therefore 2q^{2}=p^{2}\)

\(\therefore p^{2}\) is even.

\(\therefore p\) is also even, means 2 is a factor of \(p\).  ....(I)

\(\therefore p=2t\)  \(\therefore p^{2}=4t^{2}\),  \(t \in I\)

\(\therefore 2q^{2}=4t^{2}\)  (since \(p^{2}=2q^{2}\))  \(\therefore q^{2}=2t^{2}\)  \(\therefore q^{2}\) is even.  \(\therefore q\) is even.

\(\therefore\) 2 is a factor of \(q\).  ....(II)

From the statements (I) and (II), 2 is a common factor of \(p\) and \(q\) both.

This is contradictory, because in \(\frac{p}{q}\) we have assumed that \(p\) and \(q\) have no common factor except 1.

\(\therefore\) Our assumption that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational is wrong.

\(\therefore \sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.

subtopic: Irrational Numbers and the Number Line
stem: Find the square root of 2 and 3 using the division method, and hence state what kind of decimal expansion \(\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) have.
solution:
Square root of 2, by the division method on \(2.\overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ldots\):

Divisor 1, quotient digit 1: \(1\times 1=1\), remainder \(2-1=1\).
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 100\). Divisor 24, quotient digit 4: \(24\times 4=96\), remainder 4.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 400\). Divisor 281, quotient digit 1: \(281\times 1=281\), remainder 119.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 11900\). Divisor 2824, quotient digit 4: \(2824\times 4=11296\), remainder 604.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 60400\). Divisor 28282, quotient digit 2: \(28282\times 2=56564\), remainder 3836.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 383600\). Divisor 282841, quotient digit 1, and so on.

\(\therefore \sqrt{2}=1.41421\ldots\)

Square root of 3, by the division method on \(3.\overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ \overline{00}\ldots\):

Divisor 1, quotient digit 1: \(1\times 1=1\), remainder \(3-1=2\).
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 200\). Divisor 27, quotient digit 7: \(27\times 7=189\), remainder 11.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 1100\). Divisor 343, quotient digit 3: \(343\times 3=1029\), remainder 71.
Bring down \(00 \Rightarrow 7100\). Divisor 3462, quotient digit 2: \(3462\times 2=6924\), remainder 176, and so on.

\(\therefore \sqrt{3}=1.732\ldots\)

Note that in the above divisions, the numbers after the decimal point are unending, means it is non-terminating. Even no group of numbers or a single number is repeating in the quotient. So the decimal expansion of such numbers is non-terminating, non-recurring.

\(\sqrt{2},\ \sqrt{3}\) are irrational numbers, hence \(1.4142\ldots\) and \(1.732\ldots\) are irrational numbers too. Moreover, a number whose decimal expansion is non-terminating, non-recurring is irrational.

subtopic: Irrational Numbers and the Number Line
stem: We know that \(\sqrt{3}\) is an irrational number because its decimal expansion is non-terminating, non-recurring. Show whether \(2+\sqrt{3}\) is irrational or not.
solution:
Let us assume that \(2+\sqrt{3}\) is not an irrational number.

If \(2+\sqrt{3}\) is rational, then let \(2+\sqrt{3}=\frac{p}{q}\).

\(\therefore\) We get \(\sqrt{3}=\frac{p}{q}-2\).

In this equation the left side is an irrational number and the right side is a rational number, which is contradictory.

So \(2+\sqrt{3}\) is not a rational but it is an irrational number.

Similarly it can be proved that \(2\sqrt{3}\) is irrational.

stem: If the surd \(\sqrt{2}\) is multiplied by \(\sqrt{2}\), what do we get? Hence state a rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).
solution:
If surd \(\sqrt{2}\) is multiplied by \(\sqrt{2}\) we get \(\sqrt{2 \times 2} = \sqrt{4}\). \(\sqrt{4} = 2\) is a rational number.

\(\therefore\) \(\sqrt{2}\) is a rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

\(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{8} = \sqrt{16} = 4\) is a rational number.

\(\therefore\) \(\sqrt{2}\) is the rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{8}\).

Similarly \(8\sqrt{2}\) is also a rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{2}\), because \(\sqrt{2} \times 8\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = 8 \times 2 = 16\).

\(\sqrt{27} = \sqrt{9 \times 3} = 3\sqrt{3}\)

\(\therefore\) \(3\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 3 \times 3 = 9\) is a rational number.

\(\therefore\) \(\sqrt{3}\) is the rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{27}\).

Note that \(\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}\) means \(3\sqrt{3} \times 3\sqrt{3} = 9 \times 3 = 27\).

Hence \(3\sqrt{3}\) is also a rationalizing factor of \(\sqrt{27}\). In the same way \(4\sqrt{3}\), \(7\sqrt{3}\), \(\ldots\) are also the rationalizing factors of \(\sqrt{27}\). Out of all these \(\sqrt{3}\) is the simplest rationalizing factor.
